procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant-accused was convicted and sentenced to imprisonment by the Trial Court. The appellant-accused appealed to the High Court of M.P., Indore Bench (Criminal Appeal No. 309 of 2007). The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence of the appellant-accused. The High Court acquitted the co-accused.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was correct in confirming the conviction of the appellant-accused under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code.

facts: The case involved a verbal quarrel between the victim and the appellant's party.
During this quarrel, the appellant struck the victim once on the head with a 'farsi' (an axe-like weapon), causing a fatal injury.
The Trial Court convicted the appellant of murder under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC).
The High Court acquitted all other co-accused but upheld the appellant's conviction and life sentence for murder.
law: The Supreme Court focused on Exception 4 to Section 300 of the Indian Penal Code.

This exception states that culpable homicide is not murder if it is committed without premeditation, in a sudden fight, in the heat of passion upon a sudden quarrel, and provided the offender has not taken undue advantage or acted in a cruel or unusual manner.
application: The Court determined that the incident arose from a "sudden fight" following a "wordy quarrel," which established the absence of premeditation.
It noted that the appellant inflicted only a single blow to the deceased.
The Court reasoned that causing only one injury, even though it was fatal, indicated that the appellant had not taken "undue advantage" of the victim.
Based on these elements—a sudden fight without premeditation and no undue advantage taken—the Court concluded that the appellant's actions fell under Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the High Court was incorrect to confirm the conviction for murder under Section 302 IPC. Because the death occurred in a sudden fight without premeditation and the appellant did not take undue advantage, the offense was not murder but culpable homicide not amounting to murder. Therefore, the Court modified the conviction from Section 302 IPC to the lesser offense of Section 304 Part-I IPC and reduced the sentence to the time already served.

issue.issue_text: Whether the sentence of imprisonment confirmed by the High Court was appropriate.

facts: The appellant was convicted for murder under Section 302 IPC and sentenced to life imprisonment by the Trial Court, a decision affirmed by the High Court.
The incident occurred at night following a "wordy quarrel" between the accused party and the deceased.
During this quarrel, the appellant inflicted a single fatal blow with a 'farsi' to the right side of the deceased's head.
The court noted that only one significant injury was caused, indicating the appellant did not take undue advantage of the situation.
law: The Supreme Court considered Exception 4 to Section 300 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC).

This exception reduces the charge from murder to culpable homicide not amounting to murder if the act is committed without premeditation, in a sudden fight, in the heat of passion upon a sudden quarrel, and without the offender taking undue advantage or acting in a cruel manner.
application: The Court determined that the incident met the criteria of Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC.
It found that the "wordy quarrel" constituted a "sudden quarrel" which led to a "sudden fight," implying an absence of premeditation.
The fact that the appellant inflicted only one fatal blow was interpreted as evidence that he had not taken "undue advantage" of the deceased.
Therefore, the Court concluded that the offence was not murder under Section 302 IPC, but rather culpable homicide not amounting to murder.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court found the sentence of life imprisonment confirmed by the High Court to be inappropriate. It modified the appellant's conviction from murder (Section 302 IPC) to culpable homicide not amounting to murder (Section 304 Part-I IPC) and reduced the sentence to the period the appellant had already served, ordering his immediate release.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court was correct in confirming the conviction of the appellant-accused under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code.
appellant_arguments: The specific arguments of the appellant are not detailed in the provided text, but they appealed the High Court's confirmation of their conviction under Section 302 IPC.
respondent_arguments: The respondent (State) argued that the conviction was correct as the prosecution's case was based on the strong evidence of PW-6, an injured eyewitness. PW-6 testified to seeing the appellant inflict a 'farsi blow' on the deceased's head. The respondent contended that PW-6's testimony was reliable, stood on a 'higher footing' as an injured witness, and was supported by medical evidence.

cases.case_name: Abdul Sayeed v. State of M.P.
cases.principle: For the application of Exception 4 to Section 300 of the Penal Code, which deals with death caused in a sudden fight without premeditation, where the offender has not taken undue advantage.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The presence of injuries on the person of an eyewitness lends assurance to their testimony.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Court found the testimony of the injured eyewitness (PW-6) to be credible and reliable, which established the appellant's role in the fatal act. However, the Court concluded that the act did not constitute murder under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code, but rather culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Section 304 Part-I IPC, leading to a modification of the conviction and a reduction of the sentence to the time already served.
legal_tests_applied: The testimony of an injured eyewitness is considered highly reliable and provides assurance to the prosecution's case, and there must be a compelling reason to disbelieve it.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant failed to secure a full acquittal because the Court found the testimony of the injured eyewitness (PW-6) to be credible, stating, "There is no reason to disbelieve the testimony of injured eye witness(PW-6)." This testimony directly implicated the appellant in the act that caused the death.
why_respondent_won: The respondent (State) succeeded in upholding a conviction against the appellant because its case was based on the evidence of the injured eyewitness (PW-6), which the Court accepted as reliable and sufficient to establish the appellant's culpability for the death.
